studies.title: A growth hormone-releasing peptide promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and a fat burning-like phenotype through scavenger receptor CD36 in white adipocytes.
studies.abstract: Whereas the uptake of oxidized lipoproteins by scavenger receptor CD36 in macrophages has been associated with foam cell formation and atherogenesis, little is known about the role of CD36 in regulating lipid metabolism in adipocytes. Here we report that treatment of 3T3-L1 adipocytes with hexarelin, a GH-releasing peptide that interacts with CD36, resulted in a depletion of intracellular lipid content with no significant change in CD36 expression. Microarray analysis revealed an increased pattern in several genes involved in fatty acid mobilization toward the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation process in response to hexarelin. Interestingly, many of these up-regulated genes are known targets of peroxisomal proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma, such as FATP, CPT-1, and F(1)-ATPase, suggesting that adipocyte response to hexarelin may involve PPARgamma activation. Expression studies also indicate an increase in thermogenic markers PPARgamma coactivator 1alpha and uncoupling protein-1, which are normally expressed in brown adipocytes. Electron microscopy of hexarelin-treated 3T3-L1 adipocytes showed an intense and highly organized cristae formation that spans the entire width of mitochondria, compared with untreated cells, and cytochrome c oxidase activity was enhanced by hexarelin, two features characteristic of highly oxidative tissues. A similar mitochondrial phenotype was detected in epididymal white fat of mice treated with hexarelin, along with an increased expression of thermogenic markers that was lost in treated CD36-null mice, suggesting that the ability of hexarelin to promote a brown fat-like phenotype also occurs in vivo and is dependent on CD36. These results provide a potential role for CD36 to impact the overall metabolic activity of fat usage and mitochondrial biogenesis in adipocytes.

studies.title: A growth hormone-releasing peptide that binds scavenger receptor CD36 and ghrelin receptor up-regulates sterol transporters and cholesterol efflux in macrophage
studies.abstract: Macrophages play a central role in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis by accumulating cholesterol through increased uptake of oxidized low-density lipoproteins by scavenger receptor CD36, leading to foam cell formation. Here we demonstrate the ability of hexarelin, a GH-releasing peptide, to enhance the expression of ATP-binding cassette A1 and G1 transporters and cholesterol efflux in macrophages. These effects were associated with a transcriptional activation of nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)gamma in response to binding of hexarelin to CD36 and GH secretagogue-receptor 1a, the receptor for ghrelin. The hormone binding domain was not required to mediate PPARgamma activation by hexarelin, and phosphorylation of PPARgamma was increased in THP-1 macrophages treated with hexarelin, suggesting that the response to hexarelin may involve PPARgamma activation function-1 activity. However, the activation of PPARgamma by hexarelin did not lead to an increase in CD36 expression, as opposed to liver X receptor (LXR)alpha, suggesting a differential regulation of PPARgamma-targeted genes in response to hexarelin. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays showed that, in contrast to a PPARgamma agonist, the occupancy of the CD36 promoter by PPARgamma was not increased in THP-1 macrophages treated with hexarelin, whereas the LXRalpha promoter was strongly occupied by PPARgamma in the same conditions. Treatment of apolipoprotein E-null mice maintained on a lipid-rich diet with hexarelin resulted in a significant reduction in atherosclerotic lesions, concomitant with an enhanced expression of PPARgamma and LXRalpha target genes in peritoneal macrophages. The response was strongly impaired in PPARgamma(+/-) macrophages, indicating that PPARgamma was required to mediate the effect of hexarelin. These findings provide a novel mechanism by which the beneficial regulation of PPARgamma and cholesterol metabolism in macrophages could be regulated by CD36 and ghrelin receptor downstream effects.

studies.title: Endocrine, metabolic and cardioprotective effects of hexarelin in obese Zucker rats.
studies.abstract: Genetically obese male Zucker rats have an impaired secretion of GH, coupled to hyperinsulinemia, hyperlipidemia and glucose intolerance. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether a chronic treatment with hexarelin, a synthetic enkephalin-derived hexapeptide with a potent GH-releasing activity, might be able to ameliorate the somatotropic function and reverse some metabolic alterations associated with obesity in male obese Zucker rats. Furthermore, as decreased GH secretion and insulin resistance are associated with increased cardiovascular risk, we also tested the capacity of hexarelin to prevent postischemic ventricular dysfunction in hearts of male obese Zucker rats. Obese and lean male rats of the Zucker strain were treated with hexarelin (80 microgram/kg, b.i.d., s.c.) or saline (1 ml/kg, b.i.d., s.c.) for 30 days. An acute hexarelin injection (80 microgram, s.c.) at the 28th day of treatment elicited a rise in plasma GH levels in ! lean but not in obese rats (pretreated or not with hexarelin); lean rats chronically treated with hexarelin showed a greater increase in plasma GH as compared with control counterparts. At the end of the experiment, pituitary GH mRNA levels were significantly reduced in obese rats and hexarelin administration failed to increase pituitary GH mRNA and IGF-I concentrations in plasma and heart. Chronic treatment with hexarelin increased insulinemia and blood glucose levels in obese but not in lean rats, left unaltered the high triglyceride levels but significantly decreased plasma cholesterol concentrations in obese rats. Heart preparations from lean and obese Zucker rats treated with saline, subjected to low flow ischemia and reperfusion, showed at reperfusion: a) a low recovery of postischemic left ventricular developed pressure (LVDP), coupled to a substantial increase in coronary perfusion pressure, and b) a marked increase in creatine kinase released in the perfusates. Hexare! lin administration for 30 days counteracted the heart ischemic damage both in lean and obese Zucker rats. In fact, the recovery of LVDP at reperfusion was significantly higher than in controls and the increase in coronary resistance was minimal. Collectively, these data indicate that a 30-day treatment with hexarelin was unable to improve somatotropic function in male obese Zucker rats but was successful in decreasing plasma cholesterol concentrations. Hexarelin exerted a cardioprotective effect in both lean and obese rats. The heart-protective activity afforded by the peptide was divorced from any stimulation of the GH axis and is probably exerted through activation of specific cardiac receptors.

studies.title: Growth hormone-independent cardioprotective effects of hexarelin in the rat.
studies.abstract: We previously reported that induction of selective GH deficiency in the rat exacerbates cardiac dysfunction induced by experimental ischemia and reperfusion performed on the explanted heart. In the same model, short-term treatment with hexarelin, a GH-releasing peptide, reverted this effect, as did GH. To ascertain whether hexarelin had non-GH-mediated protective effects on the heart, we compared hexarelin and GH treatment in hypophysectomized rats. Hexarelin (80 microg/kg sc), given for 7 days, prevented exacerbation of the ischemia-reperfusion damage induced by hypophysectomy. We also demonstrate that hexarelin prevents increases in left ventricular end diastolic pressure, coronary perfusion pressure, reactivity of the coronary vasculature to angiotensin II, and release of creatine kinase in the heart perfusate. Moreover, hexarelin prevents the fall in prostacyclin release and enhances recovery of contractility. Treatment with GH (400 microg/kg sc) produced similar results, whereas administration of EP 51389 (80 microg/kg sc), another GH-releasing peptide that does not bind to the heart, was ineffective. In conclusion, we demonstrate that hexarelin prevents cardiac damage after ischemia-reperfusion, and that its action is not mediated by GH but likely occurs through activation of specific cardiac receptors.

studies.title: Hexarelin exhibits protective activity against cardiac ischaemia in hearts from growth hormone-deficient rats.
studies.abstract: Male rats were treated with growth hormone (GH)-releasing hormone antiserum to induce selective GH deficiency. The chronic administration of hexarelin to these GH-deficient rats had a pronounced protective effect against ischaemic and post-ischaemic ventricular dysfunction. Hexarelin prevented hyper-responsiveness of the coronary vascular bed to angiotensin II and also prevented the reduction in generation of 6-keto-prostaglandin F1alpha in perfused hearts from GH-deficient rats. The most plausible interpretation of these findings is that hexarelin acts via stimulation of specific cardiac and vascular receptors, triggering currently unknown cytoprotective mechanisms that are responsible for resistance to ischaemic insults and for the preservation of the integrity of the endothelial vasodilation function.
studies.journal: Growth hormone & IGF research : official journal of the Growth Hormone Research Society and the International IGF Research Society

studies.title: Protectant activity of hexarelin or growth hormone against postischemic ventricular dysfunction in hearts from aged rats.
studies.abstract: The ability of hexarelin, a recently synthesized hexapeptide with a strong growth hormone (GH)-releasing activity, or of GH itself to display a protectant activity against postischemic ventricular dysfunction in senescent hearts was studied in 24-month-old male rats. Heart preparations from control (saline-treated) senescent rats, subjected to moderate ischemia, showed at reperfusion: (a) a low recovery of postischemic left ventricular developed pressure (LVDP; 37% of the preischemic values; from 90 +/- 5.7 to 33.5 +/- 3.8 mm Hg; p < 0.01; n = 10) coupled to a substantial increase in coronary perfusion pressure (CPP; 71% over baseline; from 68.3 +/- 5.2 to 116.8 +/- 4.6 mm Hg; p < 0.01; n = 10); (b) a marked increase of creatine kinase (CK) released in the perfusates (6.6-fold increase over preischemic values; from 45 +/- 4 to 298 +/- 25 mU/min/g wet tissue; p < 0.001; n = 10). In vivo administration of hexarelin (80 microg/kg, b.i.d., s.c.) for 21 days resulted in a striking heart protection against reperfusion stunning. In fact, the recovery of LVDP at reperfusion was almost complete (90% of the preischemic values; from 93 +/- 5.8 to 83.7 +/- 5.9 mm Hg; p > 0.05; n = 9), and the increase in coronary resistance was minimal (from 67 +/- 5.8 to 79.7 +/- 6.9 mm Hg; p > 0.05; n = 9). Furthermore, the concentration of CK in the perfusates was increased only twofold (from 45.8 +/- 5.5 to 90 +/- 7.2 mU/min/g wet tissue; p < 0.05; n = 9), with a gradual return toward basal values at the end of reperfusion. The protectant activity of hexarelin was divorced from any detectable alteration of the somatotropic function, as assessed by pituitary GH messenger RNA (mRNA) and plasma insulin-like growth factor I levels. In vivo administration of GH (400 microg/kg b.i.d., s.c.) for the same time lapse resulted in only a partial protectant activity: 55% of LVDP recovery (from 91.5 +/- 6.2 to 50 +/- 3.5 mm Hg; p < 0.01; n = 6); 65% increase of coronary resistance (from 68 +/- 4.3 to 112.2 +/- 5.2 mm Hg; p < 0.01; n = 6); 5.3-fold increase of CK concentrations in heart perfusates on reperfusion (from 43.8 +/- 3.8 to 232 +/- 16 mU/min/g wet tissue; p < 0.001; n = 6). Evaluation of the rate of release of 6-keto-prostaglandin F1alpha (PGF1alpha), the stable metabolite of prostacyclin, in heart perfusates, and assessment of the vasopressor activity of angiotensin II on the coronary vasculature, did not show any change in these parameters among the three experimental groups. Collectively these data indicate that hexarelin displays a strong heart-protectant activity against myocardial stunning in senescent rats. The protection afforded by the peptide is likely due to a direct cardiotropic action and is far greater than that of GH. Neither compound appears able to interfere with the endothelium-dependent relaxant mechanism.

studies.title: Cardiac ischemia and impairment of vascular endothelium function in hearts from growth hormone-deficient rats: protection by hexarelin.
studies.abstract: The ability of hexarelin, an effective growth hormone (GH)-releasing hexapeptide, to reverse the worsening of cardiac dysfunction in GH-deficient animals was studied in young male rats passively immunized by administration of an anti-GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) serum. Heart preparations from anti-GHRH serum-treated rats, undergoing low-flow ischemia and reperfusion, showed: (1) a progressive increase of left ventricular end-diastolic pressure during the ischemic period and a poor recovery of contractility at reperfusion with a consistent decrease of the left ventricular-developed pressure; (2) a decreased rate of formation of 6-keto-prostaglandin F1alpha (6-keto-PGF1alpha), a stable metabolite of prostacyclin, in perfusates from preischemic and reperfusion periods; (3) an increased vasopressor activity of angiotensin II. Hexarelin (80 microg/kg, bid, s.c.), administered for 15 days to anti-GHRH serum-treated rats, restored to normal the impaired somatotropic function and counteracted the ischemic damage, improving postischemic left ventricular developed pressure to values higher than those of controls. Furthermore, both the generation of 6-keto-PGF1alpha and the vasopressor activity of angiotensin II reverted to those of control preparations. Administration of hexarelin to control rats induced a considerable improvement of postischemic ventricular function of the perfused hearts which was similar to that present in preparations from anti-GHRH serum-treated rats given hexarelin. This protective activity was divorced from any further stimulation of somatotropic function. Collectively, these data indicate that, in GH-deficient rats, hexarelin is capable of restoring somatotropic function and has a beneficial effect in myocardial ischemia and reperfusion damage. In addition, the increased responsiveness of the coronary vasculature to angiotensin II and the decreased generation of prostacyclin in hearts from GH-deficient rats would indicate that for prevention of injury and dysfunction of the vascular endothelium a normal somatotropic function is mandatory.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Synthetic peptide that mimics a natural hormone signal to release growth hormone.
explanation.what_it_is: Hexarelin is a short synthetic peptide — a chain of six amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) — designed to activate the same receptor that ghrelin, a natural stomach hormone, activates. It is injected subcutaneously (under the skin) and is not approved as a medicine in most countries; it is primarily used in research and sometimes obtained as a research chemical. It goes by several names: examorelin, EP-23905, and its chemical code 140703-51-1.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Binds a receptor on pituitary cells to trigger release of growth hormone and stress hormones.
explanation.how_it_works: Hexarelin works by plugging into a receptor called the GHS-R (growth hormone secretagogue receptor) — think of it as a molecular lock on the surface of cells in the pituitary gland, the small gland at the base of your brain that releases hormones into your bloodstream. When hexarelin binds to this lock, it sends a signal that tells those cells to release growth hormone, and also triggers release of other hormones: ACTH and cortisol (stress hormones), and prolactin (a milk-producing hormone). The mechanism is established from decades of endocrinology research. Whether long-term effects in humans differ from short acute doses is not yet clear from the studies retrieved.
explanation.safety_line: Short-term tolerability appears reasonable; long-term effects and many populations untested.
explanation.safety_detail: The human studies retrieved are short-term interventions (single doses or brief courses) and report mild or no serious adverse events in the mostly healthy or cardiac-disease populations tested. However, no adequately powered long-term safety trial has been retrieved, and hexarelin is excluded from or absent in trials of pregnancy, childhood, kidney disease, liver disease, and most chronic conditions — meaning its safety in those populations is unknown.
safety_bullets: Long-term effects untested: all human studies retrieved are acute (single-dose or very short course); no chronic safety data provided.
Excluded or unreported in: pregnancy, children, adolescents, renal/hepatic disease, diabetes, cancer — safety in these groups is unknown.
Drug interactions: not systematically studied in retrieved trials; potential interactions with hormonal medications and medications affecting pituitary function are not characterized.

As a research peptide: hexarelin is not a licensed pharmaceutical in most jurisdictions; purity, sterility, and manufacturing standards vary; use outside approved clinical trials carries unknown risks.
explanation.chem_meaning: Hexarelin is a moderately lipophilic peptide (XLogP 2.3), meaning it has some affinity for fatty environments in the body — a property that may aid absorption and penetration into tissues, but also makes it prone to binding non-specifically to proteins in blood. Its small size (887 Da) is typical for injectable peptides, and it is stable enough to be formulated for injection, though peptides are generally less stable orally than small molecules.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Studies from 1999–2004 consistently show that hexarelin injections trigger release of growth hormone, ACTH, cortisol, and prolactin in human subjects. A 2004 RCT found it decreases slow-wave sleep while stimulating GH and other hormones. A 1999 RCT reported acute cardiovascular and hormonal effects in healthy volunteers. A 1999 trial examined its action via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (the brain's main stress-hormone pathway). At least 11 studies with verified sample sizes involved roughly 243 participants, though many abstracts omit their numbers. The evidence includes animal work as well, but human RCTs from the late 1990s and early 2000s form the main basis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs from independent groups confirm the hormone-releasing effect; sample sizes are modest and no pooled meta-analysis is available, and all human data are from short acute exposures, so the grade is Moderate rather than Strong. No human evidence exists for testosterone specifically — only GH, cortisol, ACTH, and prolactin.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2002 RCT examined acute hexarelin administration in patients with coronary artery disease and measured cardiac performance. A 1999 RCT compared GH and hexarelin and measured cardiovascular effects in healthy humans. A 2001 trial (n=12) in normal subjects found growth hormone-independent cardiotropic (heart-directed) activities. A 1999 trial measured cardiac effects in hypopituitary adults. Animal studies from 2022 and 2021 show hexarelin reduces aortic aneurysm formation and has measurable effects on heart structure. Verified sample sizes across 3 human studies are modest (~43 participants total), and no long-term cardiac outcomes are reported.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Limited human evidence (4 human trials, mostly acute), small sample sizes, and indirectness (short acute dosing does not prove chronic benefit or harm). Animal evidence is supportive but does not establish clinical relevance in humans. Moderate reflects signal and consistency but low precision and no chronic data.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human study was retrieved — a 1999 clinical trial examining pituitary hormone secretion in adult patients, which included some kidney-function assessments. Animal studies from 2023 show hexarelin alleviates ischemic acute kidney injury in rodent models via a specific molecular pathway (MDM2/p53). A 2026 mouse study examined lung injury, and others looked at neuroprotection and metabolic effects, but kidney function in animals was tested in only a few studies. The human evidence is extremely limited.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses kidney outcomes; animal evidence is preliminary and does not reliably translate to humans. This outcome is graded Emerging because it is based almost entirely on animal models and a single brief human observation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All evidence is from animal models (mice, rats, or cell cultures). Studies from 2006–2021 show that hexarelin treatment alters lipid metabolism, increases fat-burning-like effects, and reduces atherosclerosis markers in insulin-resistant models. A 2019 study found it reduces oxidized LDL uptake by macrophages (immune cells involved in plaque formation). A 2017 study showed it improves lipid profiles in nonobese, insulin-resistant mice. No human lipid data were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Zero human studies; all 11 studies are animal or cell-based models. Animal lipid effects do not reliably predict human outcomes, especially in diverse genetic and metabolic contexts. This is graded Preliminary to reflect the exploratory nature of the evidence.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base consists of 33 human studies and 41 animal studies across all outcomes. Most human data come from RCTs and clinical trials conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s, focused on hormone secretion and acute cardiovascular effects in healthy volunteers or cardiac patients. Animal studies span 1999–2026 and explore mechanisms in rodent models of disease and cell cultures. The human evidence is predominantly short-term and acute; no long-term randomized trials of hexarelin in chronic conditions have been retrieved. This means confidence is moderate for short-term hormone effects but low for chronic use or conditions not directly studied.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records show hexarelin tested mainly in healthy adults, cardiac patients, and hypopituitary patients — notably absent are studies in children, adolescents, pregnant women, people with kidney or liver disease, and those with diabetes or metabolic disease. All human studies are short-term (acute dosing); no chronic administration data (weeks to months) are provided. Whether the acute hormone release translates to clinical benefit (e.g., improved strength, bone density, or body composition in humans) is not addressed by the studies given. Animal lipid and kidney effects are intriguing but unconfirmed in humans. These are visible gaps in the records provided; absence from these records does not mean the field has not studied them.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base is overwhelmingly animal studies (60 of 74 for testosterone, 14 of 19 for cardiovascular) with minimal human data, small verified sample sizes, and no pooled analyses—making it impossible to know whether observed hormonal effects translate to clinically meaningful outcomes or whether benefits outweigh risks in humans.

concerns.issue: Extreme imbalance: animal vs. human evidence
concerns.detail: For testosterone (the primary outcome), 40 of 74 studies are animal, and only 18 are RCTs in humans. For cardiovascular, 14 of 19 are animal studies with only 2 RCTs and 2 clinical trials in humans. For lipids, all 11 studies are animal-only. Animal efficacy does not reliably predict human benefit, especially for endocrine interventions where species differences in receptor expression and metabolism are substantial.

Only 11 of 74 testosterone studies report sample size, with a median of 12 and a range of 10–20 (except one n=104 study). For cardiovascular, only 3 of 19 report n, with a median of 12. A single outlier (the n=104 study) could shift any pooled estimate substantially. The engine itself notes 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger'—meaning the actual human participant count is unknown and cannot be verified against the claims.

The engine reports 'no pooled analysis confirms they agree' for testosterone and explicitly flags 'Inconsistency: several studies exist but no pooled analysis confirms they agree; held at moderate pending review.' For cardiovascular, no pooled estimate is extractable. Individual studies may show GH secretion or acute hemodynamic changes, but without synthesis, effect direction, magnitude, and heterogeneity remain opaque. Studies span 1994–2026, potentially reflecting methodological evolution or differing hexarelin formulations.

concerns.issue: Acute hormonal responses vs. sustained clinical benefit unclear
concerns.detail: Most human RCTs measure acute GH, ACTH, cortisol, and prolactin secretion in response to a single hexarelin dose (e.g., 1997 'acute administration of hexarelin stimulates GH secretion during day and night'; 1999 'acute cardiovascular and hormonal effects'). A single acute neuroendocrine stimulus does not establish efficacy for chronic use or safety. Cardiovascular studies from 1999–2002 are old; recent animal work (2020–2023) suggests cardioprotection in mouse models, but these have not been replicated in human trials.

concerns.issue: Kidney function grade 'Emerging' based on one human study
concerns.detail: Only 1 human clinical trial addresses kidney function (1999, n unreported), while 23 animal studies exist. The engine states 'consistency cannot be assessed across independent human evidence.' This outcome should not be graded above 'Anecdotal' until at least 2–3 independent human trials with adequate sample sizes and consistent endpoints exist.

concerns.issue: Funding and conflict of interest not visible
concerns.detail: No funding sources, author affiliations, or industry sponsorship are reported in the records provided. Given that hexarelin is not approved for human use and is often obtained grey-market, transparency about who funded the research and whether any authors have financial interests in promoting it is critical but absent from this evidence summary.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Hexarelin is a synthetic ghrelin-receptor agonist that robustly stimulates GH secretion in acute, controlled settings—this is biochemically sound and consistent across studies. However, the leap from acute GH/ACTH/cortisol release to sustained clinical benefit (e.g., improved cardiovascular function, kidney protection, lipid control) is large and largely unsupported by human evidence. Animal studies show cardioprotection and metabolic improvements, but these use disease models (post-ischemic dysfunction, nonobese insulin-resistant rats) with high internal validity but unknown external validity to healthy humans or patients receiving the compound chronically. No human study in this record measures long-term metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue that this is a classic case of mechanistic promise without clinical proof. The acute neuroendocrine effects are real but pharmacologically trivial—a single injection causes expected hormone release, which is not clinically meaningful. The cardiovascular and metabolic benefits observed in mice and rats over decades have failed to translate into human trials, and the oldest human RCTs are 25+ years old. The lipids outcome is 100% animal-derived, kidney function is 96% animal-derived, and even testosterone is 54% animal-derived. Without a large, recent, multi-site RCT in humans with clinically relevant endpoints (e.g., body composition, insulin sensitivity, cardiac function measured prospectively), the evidence is insufficient to support use, especially given the compound's unapproved status and potential for off-target effects.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A rigorous, multi-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in humans with (1) n ≥ 100–150, (2) chronic dosing over 12+ weeks, (3) pre-specified primary endpoints (e.g., change in lean mass, HOMA-IR, ejection fraction, or LDL), and (4) prospectively registered protocol would be needed. Secondary requirement: transparent reporting of adverse events and withdrawals, particularly cardiovascular and metabolic safety signals.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Péptido sintético que imita una señal natural de hormona para liberar hormona del crecimiento.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La hexarelina es un péptido sintético corto — una cadena de seis aminoácidos (los componentes básicos de las proteínas) — diseñado para activar el mismo receptor que la grelina, una hormona natural del estómago, activa. Se inyecta por vía subcutánea (bajo la piel) y no está aprobado como medicamento en la mayoría de los países; se utiliza principalmente en investigación y a veces se obtiene como químico de investigación. Tiene varios nombres: examorelina, EP-23905, y su código químico 140703-51-1.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Se une a un receptor en células hipofisarias para desencadenar la liberación de hormona del crecimiento y hormonas de estrés.
explanation_es.how_it_works: La hexarelina funciona enchufándose en un receptor llamado GHS-R (receptor secretagogo de hormona del crecimiento) — piénsalo como una cerradura molecular en la superficie de células en la glándula hipófisis, la pequeña glándula en la base de tu cerebro que libera hormonas en tu torrente sanguíneo. Cuando la hexarelina se une a esta cerradura, envía una señal que le dice a esas células que liberen hormona del crecimiento, y también desencadena la liberación de otras hormonas: ACTH y cortisol (hormonas de estrés), y prolactina (una hormona productora de leche). El mecanismo está establecido a partir de décadas de investigación en endocrinología. Si los efectos a largo plazo en humanos difieren de las dosis agudas cortas aún no está claro a partir de los estudios recuperados.
explanation_es.safety_line: La tolerabilidad a corto plazo parece razonable; los efectos a largo plazo y muchas poblaciones no han sido probados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los estudios en humanos recuperados son intervenciones a corto plazo (dosis únicas o cursos breves) e informan eventos adversos leves o sin efectos secundarios graves en las poblaciones principalmente sanas o con enfermedad cardíaca probadas. Sin embargo, no se ha recuperado ningún ensayo de seguridad a largo plazo adecuadamente diseñado, y la hexarelina está excluida o ausente en ensayos de embarazo, infancia, enfermedad renal, enfermedad hepática y la mayoría de condiciones crónicas — lo que significa que su seguridad en esas poblaciones es desconocida.
safety_bullets: Efectos a largo plazo no probados: todos los estudios en humanos recuperados son agudos (dosis única o curso muy breve); no se proporcionan datos de seguridad crónica.
Excluido o no informado en: embarazo, niños, adolescentes, enfermedad renal/hepática, diabetes, cáncer — la seguridad en estos grupos es desconocida.

Interacciones farmacológicas: no se han estudiado sistemáticamente en los ensayos recuperados; las posibles interacciones con medicamentos hormonales y medicamentos que afectan la función hipofisaria no están caracterizadas.

Como péptido de investigación: la hexarelina no es un fármaco licenciado en la mayoría de las jurisdicciones; la pureza, esterilidad y estándares de fabricación varían; el uso fuera de ensayos clínicos aprobados conlleva riesgos desconocidos.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La hexarelina es un péptido moderadamente lipófilo (XLogP 2.3), lo que significa que tiene cierta afinidad por ambientes grasos en el cuerpo — una propiedad que puede ayudar a la absorción e penetración en los tejidos, pero también la hace propensa a unirse inespecíficamente a proteínas en la sangre. Su pequeño tamaño (887 Da) es típico para péptidos inyectables, y es lo suficientemente estable para formularse para inyección, aunque los péptidos generalmente son menos estables por vía oral que las moléculas pequeñas.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Los estudios de 1999–2004 muestran consistentemente que las inyecciones de hexarelina desencadenan la liberación de hormona del crecimiento, ACTH, cortisol y prolactina en sujetos humanos. Un ECA de 2004 encontró que disminuye el sueño de onda lenta mientras estimula GH y otras hormonas. Un ECA de 1999 informó efectos cardiovasculares y hormonales agudos en voluntarios sanos. Un ensayo de 1999 examinó su acción a través del eje hipotálamo-hipófisis-suprarrenal (la vía principal de hormonas de estrés del cerebro). Al menos 11 estudios con tamaños de muestra verificados involucraron aproximadamente 243 participantes, aunque muchos resúmenes omiten sus números. La evidencia incluye trabajo animal también, pero los ECA humanos de finales de los años 1990 y principios de los 2000 forman la base principal.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Múltiples ECA humanos de grupos independientes confirman el efecto de liberación de hormonas; los tamaños de muestra son modestos y no hay metanálisis combinado disponible, y todos los datos humanos son de exposiciones agudas cortas, por lo que la calificación es Moderada en lugar de Fuerte. No existe evidencia humana para testosterona específicamente — solo GH, cortisol, ACTH y prolactina.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un ECA de 2002 examinó la administración aguda de hexarelina en pacientes con enfermedad de las arterias coronarias y midió el rendimiento cardíaco. Un ECA de 1999 comparó GH y hexarelina y midió efectos cardiovasculares en humanos sanos. Un ensayo de 2001 (n=12) en sujetos normales encontró actividades cardiotropas (dirigidas al corazón) independientes de la hormona del crecimiento. Un ensayo de 1999 midió efectos cardíacos en adultos hipopituitarios. Los estudios en animales de 2022 y 2021 muestran que la hexarelina reduce la formación de aneurisma aórtico y tiene efectos medibles en la estructura del corazón. Los tamaños de muestra verificados en 3 estudios humanos son modestos (~43 participantes en total), y no se informan resultados cardíacos a largo plazo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidencia humana limitada (4 ensayos humanos, principalmente agudos), tamaños de muestra pequeños e indirectitud (dosis aguda corta no prueba beneficio o daño crónico). La evidencia en animales es de apoyo pero no establece relevancia clínica en humanos. Moderada refleja señal y consistencia pero baja precisión y sin datos crónicos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo se recuperó un estudio humano — un ensayo clínico de 1999 que examinaba la secreción de hormonas hipofisarias en pacientes adultos, que incluía algunas evaluaciones de función renal. Los estudios en animales de 2023 muestran que la hexarelina alivia la lesión renal aguda isquémica en modelos de roedores a través de una vía molecular específica (MDM2/p53). Un estudio en ratones de 2026 examinó lesión pulmonar, y otros analizaron neuroprotección y efectos metabólicos, pero la función renal en animales fue probada en solo algunos estudios. La evidencia humana es extremadamente limitada.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un estudio humano aborda resultados renales; la evidencia animal es preliminar y no se traduce de manera confiable a humanos. Este resultado se califica como Emergente porque se basa casi enteramente en modelos animales y una observación humana breve única.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Toda la evidencia proviene de modelos en animales (ratones, ratas o cultivos celulares). Los estudios de 2006–2021 muestran que el tratamiento con hexarelina altera el metabolismo de lípidos, aumenta efectos similares a la quema de grasa y reduce marcadores de aterosclerosis en modelos resistentes a la insulina. Un estudio de 2019 encontró que reduce la captación de LDL oxidado por macrófagos (células inmunes involucradas en la formación de placa). Un estudio de 2017 mostró que mejora los perfiles de lípidos en ratones no obesos e insulinorresistentes. No se recuperaron datos de lípidos humanos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Cero estudios humanos; los 11 estudios son modelos basados en animales o cultivos celulares. Los efectos de lípidos en animales no predicen de manera confiable los resultados humanos, especialmente en contextos genéticos y metabólicos diversos. Esto se califica como Preliminar para reflejar la naturaleza exploratoria de la evidencia.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia consta de 33 estudios humanos y 41 estudios en animales en todos los resultados. La mayoría de los datos humanos provienen de ECA y ensayos clínicos realizados a finales de los años 1990 y principios de los 2000, enfocados en secreción de hormonas y efectos cardiovasculares agudos en voluntarios sanos o pacientes cardíacos. Los estudios en animales abarcan 1999–2026 e exploran mecanismos en modelos de enfermedad de roedores y cultivos celulares. La evidencia humana es predominantemente a corto plazo y aguda; no se ha recuperado ningún ensayo randomizado a largo plazo de hexarelina en condiciones crónicas. Esto significa que la confianza es moderada para efectos hormonales a corto plazo pero baja para uso crónico o condiciones no estudiadas directamente.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados muestran hexarelina probada principalmente en adultos sanos, pacientes cardíacos y pacientes hipopituitarios — notablemente ausentes están los estudios en niños, adolescentes, mujeres embarazadas, personas con enfermedad renal o hepática y aquellos con diabetes o enfermedad metabólica. Todos los estudios humanos son a corto plazo (dosis aguda); no se proporcionan datos de administración crónica (semanas a meses). Si la liberación de hormona aguda se traduce en beneficio clínico (p. ej., mejora de la fuerza, densidad ósea o composición corporal en humanos) no se aborda en los estudios dados. Los efectos renales y de lípidos en animales son intrigantes pero sin confirmar en humanos. Estas son brechas visibles en los registros proporcionados; la ausencia de estos registros no significa que el campo no los haya estudiado.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia está abrumadoramente dominada por estudios en animales (60 de 74 para testosterona, 14 de 19 para cardiovascular) con datos humanos mínimos, tamaños de muestra verificados pequeños, y sin análisis agrupados—lo que hace imposible saber si los efectos hormonales observados se traducen en resultados clínicamente significativos o si los beneficios superan los riesgos en humanos.

concerns.issue: Desequilibrio extremo: evidencia animal vs. humana
concerns.detail: Para testosterona (el resultado primario), 40 de 74 estudios son en animales, y solo 18 son ECA en humanos. Para cardiovascular, 14 de 19 son estudios en animales con solo 2 ECA y 2 ensayos clínicos en humanos. Para lípidos, los 11 estudios son solo en animales. La eficacia animal no predice de manera confiable el beneficio humano, especialmente para intervenciones endocrinas donde las diferencias de especies en la expresión de receptores y el metabolismo son sustanciales.

Solo 11 de 74 estudios de testosterona reportan tamaño de muestra, con una mediana de 12 y un rango de 10–20 (excepto un estudio con n=104). Para cardiovascular, solo 3 de 19 reportan n, con una mediana de 12. Un único valor atípico (el estudio con n=104) podría cambiar sustancialmente cualquier estimación agrupada. El motor en sí señala 'la mayoría de los resúmenes omiten el tamaño de muestra, por lo que el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor'—lo que significa que el recuento real de participantes humanos es desconocido y no puede ser verificado contra las afirmaciones.

concerns.issue: Sin metanálisis agrupados; inconsistencia sin resolver
concerns.detail: El motor reporta 'sin análisis agrupado confirma que concuerden' para testosterona y explícitamente señala 'Inconsistencia: existen varios estudios pero sin análisis agrupado que confirme que concuerden; mantenido en moderado pendiente de revisión.' Para cardiovascular, ninguna estimación agrupada es extraíble. Los estudios individuales pueden mostrar secreción de GH o cambios hemodinámicos agudos, pero sin síntesis, la dirección del efecto, la magnitud y la heterogeneidad permanecen opacas. Los estudios abarcan 1994–2026, potencialmente reflejando evolución metodológica o diferentes formulaciones de hexarelina.

concerns.issue: Respuestas hormonales agudas vs. beneficio clínico sostenido sin claridad
concerns.detail: La mayoría de los ECA humanos miden la secreción aguda de GH, ACTH, cortisol y prolactina en respuesta a una dosis única de hexarelina (p. ej., 1997 'la administración aguda de hexarelina estimula la secreción de GH durante el día y la noche'; 1999 'efectos cardiovasculares y hormonales agudos'). Un único estímulo neuroendocrino agudo no establece eficacia para uso crónico o seguridad. Los estudios cardiovasculares de 1999–2002 son antiguos; el trabajo animal reciente (2020–2023) sugiere cardioprotección en modelos murinos, pero estos no han sido replicados en ensayos humanos.

concerns.issue: Calificación de función renal 'Emergente' basada en un estudio humano
concerns.detail: Solo 1 ensayo clínico humano aborda la función renal (1999, n no reportado), mientras que existen 23 estudios en animales. El motor indica 'la consistencia no puede ser evaluada entre evidencia humana independiente.' Este resultado no debe ser calificado por encima de 'Anecdótico' hasta que existan al menos 2–3 ensayos humanos independientes con tamaños de muestra adecuados y puntos finales consistentes.

concerns.issue: Financiamiento y conflicto de intereses no visible
concerns.detail: No se reportan fuentes de financiamiento, afiliaciones de autores, o patrocinio industrial en los registros proporcionados. Dado que la hexarelina no está aprobada para uso humano y a menudo se obtiene en el mercado gris, la transparencia sobre quién financió la investigación y si algún autor tiene intereses financieros en promoverla es crítica pero ausente en este resumen de evidencia.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: La hexarelina es un agonista sintético del receptor de ghrelina que robustamente estimula la secreción de GH en configuraciones agudas y controladas—esto es bioquímicamente correcto y consistente en los estudios. Sin embargo, el salto de la liberación aguda de GH/ACTH/cortisol al beneficio clínico sostenido (p. ej., función cardiovascular mejorada, protección renal, control de lípidos) es grande y en gran medida no respaldado por evidencia humana. Los estudios en animales muestran cardioprotección y mejoras metabólicas, pero utilizan modelos de enfermedad (disfunción post-isquémica, ratas resistentes a insulina no obesas) con alta validez interna pero validez externa desconocida en humanos sanos o pacientes que reciben el compuesto crónicamente. Ningún estudio humano en este registro mide resultados metabólicos o cardiovasculares a largo plazo.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría que este es un caso clásico de promesa mecanística sin prueba clínica. Los efectos neuroendocrinos agudos son reales pero farmacológicamente triviales—una inyección única causa liberación hormonal esperada, que no es clínicamente significativa. Los beneficios cardiovasculares y metabólicos observados en ratones y ratas durante décadas no han logrado traducirse en ensayos humanos, y los ECA humanos más antiguos tienen más de 25 años. El resultado de lípidos es 100% derivado de animales, la función renal es 96% derivada de animales, e incluso la testosterona es 54% derivada de animales. Sin un ECA grande, reciente, de múltiples sitios en humanos con puntos finales clínicamente relevantes (p. ej., composición corporal, sensibilidad a la insulina, función cardíaca medida prospectivamente), la evidencia es insuficiente para respaldar el uso, especialmente dado el estado no aprobado del compuesto y el potencial de efectos fuera del objetivo.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Se necesitaría un ECA riguroso, multicéntrico, doble ciego, controlado con placebo en humanos con (1) n ≥ 100–150, (2) dosificación crónica durante 12+ semanas, (3) puntos finales primarios preespecificados (p. ej., cambio en masa magra, HOMA-IR, fracción de eyección, o LDL), y (4) protocolo registrado prospectivamente. Requisito secundario: reporte transparente de eventos adversos y retiros, particularmente señales de seguridad cardiovascular y metabólica.
